The wizard composes your first scenario in seven short pages. A test case is one combination of values: the wizard asks what varies and what kind of thing each is (a static parameter, a sequence of actions or a sudden action), how one test case uses it, what must not happen, how many test cases are enough, and what the bootstrap prepares once, first, for all of them. Every answer shows at once how many test cases it makes; nothing runs until you choose to.

A factor is one thing that varies between test cases; its values are what it can be. Say what kind it is: a static parameter is set before any action, like the browser (chrome, firefox, safari); a sequence of actions is done in order, like the steps of a workflow (login, search, pay); a sudden action may or may not happen, like a timeout. A selection treats them apart: pairwise covers the static parameters. Each factor becomes a sheet of the scenario and each value a row of it.

path: 0.2 · Factors / Factors of the scenario: their values, how a test case uses them and their ways
name: Factors of the scenario: their values, how a test case uses them and their ways
Values are plain words; a value may hold spaces but no quote, backslash or comma. Rules and the test cases' results name them as you write them.

For each factor, say how one test case uses its values. The wizard answers with the instructions of the factor's FW_Seq row: the verb is dictated by the shape of the freedom, never chosen to hit a number.
How many of its values does one test case use?

Rules, the sieve, remove combinations before any test runs. Write one when a combination cannot happen or makes no sense for your system, like safari on linux, or paying with nothing in the cart. Do not write rules to have fewer test cases: a rule that removes valid combinations can hide a defect. When valid combinations are only too many, keep them and let a selection choose (page 0.5); when a factor is freer than it really is, change its answers (page 0.3).
Add factors first (page 0.2): a rule relates two of their values.

path: 0.4 · Rules (sieve) / Rules of the scenario, in words and as the constraints file writes them
name: Rules of the scenario, in words and as the constraints file writes them
The rules are saved beside the scenario as <name>.constraints.json; step 4 opens that file to draw more rules and shows how many test cases each one removes.

Rules decide which combinations may happen; the selection decides how many of them to try. Pairwise is for static parameters: it keeps fewer test cases while every value of each meets every value of every other in at least one of them, and most defects come from one value or two values together. Sequences of actions and sudden actions are of another kind: each kept combination runs every order of a sequence, and every sudden action happens or not, in every combination with the others.

path: 0.5 · How many / How many, and what fits
name: How many, and what fits
The selection is a run setting: Use it in step 3 puts it into step 3's run settings, and the scenario's .properties file keeps it for the command line.

The bootstrap, FW_RunMeFirstOnce, is not a factor and is never combined: it runs once, and really first, for the whole bunch of test cases a run executes after it. Put there what they all share: start or check the system you test, read a configuration, seed data, and do it so that running it again changes nothing. It receives the FW_Arguments line, and the FW_ARGS it leaves, split at spaces, is what every test case's main receives (the test cases keep it in shared). What varies between test cases belongs in factors, never in the bootstrap.

What to pick
